title: Mortgage Rates Hit 2026 High as Treasury Yields Flash Warning for Homebuyers
excerpt: The 30-year fixed rate jumped to 6.85%, with economists warning 7% is back on the table as the Iran war drives oil past $100 and Treasury yields to 18-month highs.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 30-year fixed mortgage rates reached 6.85%, the highest since mid-July 2025.
  • 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 4.7%, its highest since January 2025.
  • Economists warn that mortgage rates could hit 7% if Treasury yields approach 5%.
  • Median U.S. home price hit a record $440,600, while existing home sales fell 2.4%.

Treasury Yields Surge on Oil and Inflation Fears

The U.S. housing market received another blow this week as mortgage rates surged to their highest level of 2026, fueled by a sharp selloff in Treasury bonds that shows no signs of easing.

https://x.com/USronaldcarter/status/2080339899606003716

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped 8 basis points to 6.85% on Thursday, according to Mortgage News Daily, the highest reading since mid-July 2025. Separately, Freddie Mac reported the 30-year rate averaging 6.58% for the week ending July 23 — also a 2026 high — though its data collection period ended before Thursday's bond market rout.

The catalyst: the 10-year Treasury yield, the benchmark that drives mortgage pricing, surged past 4.7% on Thursday morning, its highest since January 2025. Treasury yields have risen more than a quarter percentage point since late June, according to Reuters, with the moves accelerating after Yemen's Houthi militants claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, pushing crude past $100 a barrel.

"Given what's happened in just recent days with the 10-year Treasury, I think mortgage rates will get closer to 7% in the coming weeks."

— Mark Fleming, Chief Economist, First American

The Iran War's Toll on Housing

Mortgage rates have climbed 0.60 percentage points since the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran in late February, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. The conflict has driven up global oil prices, feeding broader inflation that now runs at roughly twice the Federal Reserve's 2% target.

A brief respite came in June when on-again, off-again peace talks eased energy costs. But the resumption of hostilities has reversed those gains, intensifying concerns among Fed officials that they may need to raise rates to contain inflation.

"Incoming data showed that inflation dropped in June, but with oil prices spiking again, that improvement seems unlikely to continue in July data, and mortgage rates are likely to remain higher as a result," MBA Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni said.

The Fed meets next week. While a rate hike remains an outlier probability for that meeting, interest rate futures markets are positioning for at least one 25-basis-point increase from the current 3.50%–3.75% policy rate range by year-end.

Is 7% Coming Back?

The last time 30-year mortgage rates topped 7% was January 2025, when the 10-year Treasury yield sat near 4.6%. With yields now above that threshold, the question looms.

"If the 10-year Treasury yield approaches 5%, then 7% 30-year fixed mortgage rates are certainly in play," Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told MarketWatch. But the spread between Treasury yields and mortgage rates has narrowed since then, offering a slim buffer.

Impact of Rising Rates on Homebuyers
›70% of recent homebuyers expect rates to fall.
›50% say their mortgage could become financially unsustainable.
›32% have cut spending on necessities to manage payments.

Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist at Bright MLS, called 7% "possible" but "not likely," noting that lenders must price competitively in a market where transaction volumes remain historically low.

"It's hard to rule anything out," Orphe Divounguy, a senior economist at Zillow, told MarketWatch. "If the pressure on oil prices remains, mortgage rates for the rest of the year could be higher than last year's level."

A Housing Market Already Under Strain

The timing could hardly be worse. The real-estate industry had hoped the spring selling season would shake loose a market frozen since 2022. Instead, existing home sales slid 2.4% in June to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.09 million — well below expectations — according to the National Association of Realtors. The median price for a previously owned home hit a record $440,600.

The pain extends beyond mortgage rates. A Truework survey found that more than 70% of recent homebuyers were counting on rates to fall, and half said their mortgage could become "financially unsustainable" without refinancing. About 32% reported cutting spending on necessities including food, clothing, and healthcare to keep up with payments.

What Diaspora Buyers Should Watch

For NRIs considering U.S. property purchases or refinancing existing homes, the calculus has shifted. Higher rates mean steeper monthly payments, reduced buying power, and a longer wait for refinancing relief. The iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF fell 1.6% on Thursday as the housing sector repriced around rising yields.

The next signpost: the Federal Reserve's meeting next week and the trajectory of oil prices. If crude remains above $100 and Treasury yields keep climbing, the housing market's four-year slump could deepen further.
